opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we're further away than a lot of people imagine, and I've been saying this for a while. There's a paradox, which people call Moravec's paradox: we have systems that can pass the bar exam, write code, and manipulate language very fluently, but we don't have a robot that can clear the dinner table and fill the dishwasher, something any ten-year-old learns in one shot. We don't even have level-five self-driving cars, even though a teenager learns to drive in about twenty hours of practice.

That tells you something very important. We're missing something big. Language is in some sense easy, because it's discrete and it's a compressed representation of knowledge. The real world is continuous, high-dimensional, noisy, and largely unpredictable. A four-year-old has seen about as much data through vision as the largest LLMs have been trained on in text. Most of what we know about the world, intuitive physics, how objects behave, what happens if you push something, we learn from observation, not from language.

So to have useful domestic robots, we need systems that understand the physical world, that have persistent memory, that can reason, and above all that can plan: imagine the consequences of a sequence of actions and choose the one that accomplishes a task. That requires what I call world models. And I don't think you get them by training generative models to predict pixels. That doesn't work very well because the world is not entirely predictable. You need architectures like JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, that predict in an abstract representation space where you can ignore the details that aren't predictable or relevant.

Now, on the trustworthy part, I actually think this kind of architecture helps. If your system works by planning, optimizing its actions to satisfy objectives, you can build guardrails directly into those objectives. Don't run with a knife in your hand when there's a person nearby, that kind of thing. By construction, the system can't violate those constraints. That's much more controllable than an autoregressive LLM, where you just hope fine-tuning covered all the cases.

As for timing, I think we'll see real progress in the next three to five years on the fundamental science, systems that learn world models from video and interaction. But getting from there to a robot in your home that's reliable, affordable, and that you'd trust around your kids or your grandmother, that's going to take longer. There are a lot of companies building humanoid robots right now, and the hardware is getting quite good, but frankly, many of them are betting that AI will make enough progress to make those robots smart. The hardware is not really the bottleneck. The bottleneck is the intelligence.

So I'm optimistic it will happen, and it may well happen within the next decade, but it won't come from scaling up LLMs. It will require a new paradigm.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current robots cannot handle basic household tasks and that companies are betting on future AI progress to make their robots smart, indicating that none currently knows how to make them intelligent enough for useful home deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're further away than a lot of people would like to believe, and I say that as someone who is extremely enthusiastic about the long-term prospects.

The thing to understand is that the hard part of a domestic robot is not the hardware. We've had robots that can walk, manipulate objects, open doors, for a while now, and the hardware keeps getting cheaper. The hard part is that a robot in your kitchen has to deal with the real world, and the real world is not like the internet. You can't just scrape a billion examples of someone loading a dishwasher in a cluttered kitchen with a cat walking by. The robot has to understand how the physical world works: that if I push this glass it will fall, that liquids spill, that a towel folds in a way that's basically impossible to predict precisely. That's common sense, and we don't know how to give machines common sense yet.

This is why I keep saying that LLMs are not the path to this. They're trained on text, and text is a very low-bandwidth, very impoverished representation of reality. A four-year-old has absorbed more information through vision than the biggest LLM has seen in text, by orders of magnitude. And that child can learn to clear the table in a few demonstrations. Our systems can't do that. They need enormous amounts of data or very narrow training, and then they fail the moment the situation deviates.

So what's missing is a system that learns a model of the world from observation, mostly from video, in a self-supervised way, and then uses that model to plan: to imagine the consequences of actions before taking them. That's what my group has been working on with JEPA-style architectures. We're making progress, but it's research. We don't have it yet.

If you ask me for a timeline, I'd say in the next few years you'll see robots doing specific, constrained tasks in homes, in a kind of brittle way, maybe with teleoperation behind the scenes more often than companies admit. A truly general domestic robot you can trust, that you can show something once and it figures it out, that requires a breakthrough in how machines learn, not just scaling. Could be ten years, could be longer. I've been wrong about timelines before, usually by being too optimistic. But the direction is clear to me, even if the date isn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says current systems lack common sense and that a truly general, trustworthy domestic robot is still out of reach, but it does not assert that no company knows how to make robots useful in the home. It even anticipates robots doing specific constrained home tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still missing some important pieces. We have robots that can do very impressive things in controlled environments. But a home is much more complicated. Every home is different, objects move around, and there are children and pets. A robot has to handle situations that its designers didn’t anticipate.

The difficulty is not just building the hardware. It’s giving the machine enough understanding of the physical world to predict the consequences of its actions and plan safely. If you ask it to clear the dinner table, it needs to know that picking up a plate at the wrong angle might spill something, or that a glass hidden behind another object could get knocked over. Those things seem obvious to us because we’ve learned an enormous amount about the world.

So I don’t think you get a reliable domestic robot simply by putting a language model in a robot body. You need systems that learn models of the world, that can reason about what might happen, and that can recognize when they don’t know enough to act.

We’ll see useful robots for relatively narrow tasks before we see a general-purpose household assistant. But a robot you can trust to do all kinds of things in an unfamiliar home? There’s still substantial research to do. I wouldn’t give you a precise date.

r001.rationale: The candidate says domestic robots still need substantial research and will first handle narrow tasks, but it does not assert that no company building robots currently knows how to make them useful in the home.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still missing some important ideas. We have robots that can do very impressive things in a controlled environment, but a home is a very different situation. Every home is different, objects move around, and there are children and pets. You need a system that can deal with situations it has never encountered without doing something dangerous.

The difficulty is not just building the hardware. It’s giving the machine enough understanding of the physical world to predict the consequences of its actions. If it moves a table, what happens to the objects on top? If it encounters an obstacle, can it figure out another way to accomplish the task? That requires some form of world model, together with the ability to plan.

So I’m optimistic that we’ll get there, but I wouldn’t give you a reliable date. We’ll see useful robots for relatively narrow tasks first. A robot that you can leave alone in an unfamiliar house and trust to do a wide variety of chores—that’s a substantially harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response says home robotics still needs important ideas and that broadly capable, trustworthy domestic robots are difficult. It does not assert that no company currently knows how to make robots intelligent enough to be useful in the home.
